articles.title: One Laptop, Eight Models: The Dense Rows Read Memory at 89% of the Ceiling, the MoE Rows at 43-67%
articles.excerpt: A reader with a Surface Laptop Ultra sent me a table of eight local LLMs on the same machine, same llama.cpp build, same commands, speculative decoding off. His numbers are generation speed, which is…
articles.body: A reader with a Surface Laptop Ultra sent me a table of eight local LLMs on the same machine, same llama.cpp build, same commands, speculative decoding off. His numbers are generation speed, which is a memory-bandwidth result if you treat it right. So I treated it right. I turned every row into bytes per second: file size divided by total parameters gives bytes per parameter, active parameters times that gives the bytes a token has to read, and that times tokens per second gives the read rate. The dense rows land at 261.6, 264.6 and 272.2 GB/s on a machine NVIDIA rates at 300 . Three different file sizes, three different speeds, one ceiling. The MoE rows land between 114.3 and 177.4 GB/s , which is 38-59% of spec. Same laptop, same build. That gap is not noise. It is what routing costs.

articles.title: Building Introworth: Net Worth Is a Trend Line, Not a Verdict. What Worked, What Broke
articles.excerpt: A bank balance is a photograph. Net worth, written down on the same date each month, is the film. The balance jumps before rent leaves and drops the day bills land, so judging progress by it is like j…
articles.body: A bank balance is a photograph. Net worth, written down on the same date each month, is the film. The balance jumps before rent leaves and drops the day bills land, so judging progress by it is like judging a journey by a single frame. Direction is the information a household actually needs, and direction only appears when the same calculation is repeated without changing the rules. Building a tracker around that idea sounded straightforward. List everything owned, list everything owed, subtract the second total from the first, date the result, and close the page until next month. In practice, keeping people on that boring rhythm was harder than the arithmetic, and several early choices made the number feel like a verdict instead of a steering tool.

articles.title: Build an Arrow Puzzle Game in Flutter
articles.excerpt: When I built KnotGlide, a calm arrow puzzle game, the whole game rested on one simple move: tap an arrow whose path is clear and it glides out of the maze along its own route. A blocked arrow nudges f…
articles.body: When I built KnotGlide, a calm arrow puzzle game, the whole game rested on one simple move: tap an arrow whose path is clear and it glides out of the maze along its own route. A blocked arrow nudges forward and shows what is in its way, so every tap teaches the next move. The game ships with 100 curated levels in 8 chapters, a daily puzzle, time challenges and an endless mode — all fully offline, with no account and no purchases. You can see the finished game in the KnotGlide case study . This guide shows how to build that kind of game in Flutter: model the board as plain Dart data, write the clear-path check, animate the glide, handle ambiguous taps fairly, design levels that are always solvable, and add a daily puzzle with streaks — all on-device, with no network at all.

When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13) during the Starship Flight 15 test.
articles.body: Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that." SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.
articles.body: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.
